claims.text: In situ high-temperature mechanical testing with real-time synchrotron X-ray scattering or electron microscopy will reveal active deformation mechanisms in FeNiCrMn HEA.
Real-time imaging will identify strengthening pathways that increase yield strength and ductility relative to conventional ex situ testing.
The proposed FeNiCrMn material is in a homogenized or as-cast condition.
The initial FeNiCrMn material is free of major second phases.
Incremental uniaxial tensile or compressive loading should be combined with real-time high-energy synchrotron diffraction or in situ electron microscopy.
Testing at approximately 800–1000 °C mimics relevant aerospace or automotive operating conditions.
Dislocations, twins, and other defects form and interact under stress and elevated temperature in the relevant HEA.
The evolution of dislocations, twins, and defects can be tracked in real time using the proposed characterization methods.
Dislocation slip, twinning, and recrystallization are temperature-dependent processes that control mechanical behavior.
Direct observation of dynamic microstructure evolution will clarify which microscopic processes control the mechanical properties of FeNiCrMn.
The resulting mechanistic information will guide optimization of FeNiCrMn processing and composition.
Targeted thermomechanical processing selected from real-time observations will substantially enhance both yield strength and ductility.
The optimized material will surpass the performance observed in standard ex situ tests.
Prior conventional mechanical tests have characterized temperature-dependent behavior and deformation mechanisms in CoCrFeMnNi Cantor alloy.
Prior ex situ mechanical studies provide a baseline for FeNiCrMn.
The proposed real-time measurements require sophisticated facilities whose availability and cost may limit the method.
Compositional variation within FeNiCrMn may alter the observed deformation mechanisms.

The relative contributions of dislocation activity, twinning, and phase transformations to high-temperature strength in FeNiCrMn remain unquantified and may vary with composition and processing history.
